appraisal_events.evidence: Aimé, avec un éclat modeste, dégageait...le romanesque qui émane...de cheveux légers et d'un nez grec, grâce à quoi il se distinguait au milieu de la foule des autres serviteurs; il avait un air intelligent, énergique, mais respectueux.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator singles Aimé out among the restaurant's grotesque, comically aged waiters, attributing to him romantic distinction, intelligence, and quiet dignity.

appraisal_events.evidence: après avoir renvoyé Aimé assez brusquement...j'ai tout de même le droit de te mettre en garde contre ce larbin que je connais de Balbec...et qui est une des plus grandes fripouilles que la terre ait jamais portées.
appraisal_events.explanation: The moment he notices Zézette's lingering gaze at Aimé, Robert abruptly dismisses him and denounces him as a scoundrel; the narration frames this outburst as driven by jealousy rather than genuine judgment.

status_effects.explanation: Aimé is elevated above the other, grotesque old waiters through the narrator's admiring physical and moral portrait.
Robert publicly brands him a scoundrel to Zézette, locally damaging his standing even though the accusation is plainly jealousy-driven rather than substantiated.

Robert's abrupt hostility toward a waiter he otherwise knows and likes exposes his jealousy and loss of composure (the faint, telltale blush), diminishing him locally even as he tries to assert authority over Zézette.
Zézette's flat rejoinder ('Voilà que ça commence, j'en étais sûre !') shows she anticipates and names Robert's predictable jealousy, giving her the upper hand in reading him.

ambiguities: Robert's accusation against Aimé is framed by the narrator's admiring earlier description and by the established pattern of his baseless jealousy, so it is unclear whether the blame should be read as a genuine local discredit of Aimé or primarily as an exposure of Robert's own insecurity.
